screens.title: Nginx Web Server Configuration and Reverse Proxy
screens.subtitle: Install, configure server blocks, proxy requests, and implement basic load balancing.

narration.text: In this lesson you will gain practical mastery of Nginx as both a web server and an edge reverse proxy. We start with how Nginx is installed on RHEL and Debian families, then examine the configuration model — the main nginx. conf, server blocks, and location handling. You will see concrete examples for serving static files and for forwarding requests to backend application servers using proxy_pass and proxy_set_header. We explain how to validate configs with the nginx -t command, reload safely, and avoid common operational mistakes like wrong document roots, missing headers, firewall blocks, or SELinux restrictions. You will also learn a basic load balancing pattern using an upstream block so a single Nginx front end can distribute requests across multiple backends. Each concept is paired with configuration samples and a short lab that recreates a static site and a proxied Flask app. By the end you will understand when to use Nginx versus Apache, how to pass real client information to backends, and the simple checks that prevent downtime. Think about which role you will use Nginx for first — serving static assets at scale or fronting dynamic application servers — and why that choice matters.

keyIdea.title: Why Nginx matters
keyIdea.text: Nginx combines an event-driven architecture with flexible server blocks and proxy directives, making it an efficient front-end for static content, SSL termination, reverse proxying, and simple load balancing.

screens.title: Nginx Architecture — Event-Driven Model
screens.subtitle: Why Nginx handles high concurrency efficiently

narration.text: Nginx uses an event-driven, asynchronous architecture meaning a small number of worker processes can manage many thousands of concurrent connections without dedicating one process or thread per connection. In practice this means Nginx allocates workers that respond to events — such as readable sockets, writable sockets, or timer expirations — and then handles input and output in a non-blocking manner. A concrete example: serving static image assets to many clients typically benefits from Nginx because workers read and send file data without creating a separate process per client. A common misconception is that Nginx is always 'faster' than Apache for every workload; the correct nuance is that Nginx is more efficient for high-concurrency and static-serving use cases, while Apache can be preferable for some dynamic workloads that rely on per-request process models or. htaccess-style per-directory overrides. Why this matters operationally: understanding the model informs choices like worker_processes tuning, use of sendfile and caching, and deciding when to place Nginx in front of an application server. A final question to consider: when your application is C P U-bound versus input and output-bound, how does that affect whether Nginx should be the edge server or whether you should also tune backend processes?

keyIdea.title: Event-driven benefit
keyIdea.text: Event-driven processing lets Nginx handle high concurrency with fewer resources, making it ideal for static content and edge proxying.

content.html:
Core Concept

Event-driven, non-blocking I/O

Nginx uses worker processes that multiplex many connections through event loops instead of one process per connection.

Definition
Non-blocking I/O and event loops allow a single worker to manage many sockets efficiently.
Concrete example
Serving static images to thousands of clients uses few workers because operations are I/O-bound, not CPU-bound.
Common misconception
Nginx isn't always the fastest for every workload—dynamic, CPU-heavy requests may still rely on backend process models.
Key Takeaway

Use Nginx at the edge for high-concurrency, I/O-heavy workloads and front dynamic backends with a proxy to combine strengths.

Operational pointers
  • Tune worker_processes and worker_connections according to CPU and expected concurrency.
  • Enable sendfile and use appropriate buffer sizes for efficient static file serving.
  • Place Nginx as a proxy in front of application servers for SSL termination and caching when helpful.
Quick check
If your server is I/O-bound and serving many idle connections, prefer Nginx at the edge. If application logic needs per-request process features, evaluate trade-offs.

screens.title: Installing Nginx on RHEL and Debian Systems
screens.subtitle: Commands and immediate post-install checks

narration.text: Installing Nginx differs slightly between RHEL-family systems and Debian-family systems. On RHEL families you may need to enable EPEL first and then install the nginx package. After installation, enable and start the service and open HTTP and HTTPS at the firewall. On Debian families, Nginx is often available directly from apt; update package lists, install nginx, enable and start the service, and allow the 'Nginx Full' profile through UFW. A concrete example: on RHEL you run commands that add EPEL, then sudo dnf install nginx, then sudo systemctl enable --now nginx, and update firewall-cmd rules. On Debian, run sudo apt update, sudo apt install nginx, then sudo systemctl enable --now nginx and sudo ufw allow 'Nginx Full'. Always verify the daemon is active with systemctl status nginx and test reachability with curl or a browser. A common oversight is enabling the service without opening the firewall or forgetting to enable EPEL on RHEL, which prevents package installation. The key operational step is to validate that Nginx is running and reachable before modifying configuration files. Installing Nginx on RHEL and Debian Systems means enable epel on rhel when needed, install the nginx package, enable the service, open firewall ports, and verify with systemctl and curl.. In practical terms, commands and immediate post-install checks. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Install checklist
keyIdea.text: Enable EPEL on RHEL when needed, install the nginx package, enable the service, open firewall ports, and verify with systemctl and curl.

content.html:
Process Flow

Install and verify

Follow a short sequence: install, enable, open firewall, verify service and connectivity.

RHEL-family commands
sudo dnf install epel-release -y
sudo dnf install nginx -y
sudo systemctl enable nginx --now
sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --add-service=http
sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --add-service=https
sudo firewall-cmd --reload
Debian-family commands
sudo apt update
sudo apt install nginx -y
sudo systemctl enable nginx --now
sudo ufw allow 'Nginx Full'
sudo ufw enable
Common mistake
Installing without opening firewall ports or forgetting to enable EPEL prevents installation or external access.
Key Takeaway

Follow install → enable → firewall → verify steps and confirm the daemon is active before continuing to config changes.

screens.title: Nginx Configuration Files and Main Directives
screens.subtitle: Understanding nginx.conf, server blocks, and directive roles

narration.text: Nginx centralizes configuration in the main nginx. conf file, which contains global settings like the user Nginx runs as, worker_processes, and the events block. Server-specific settings are placed in server blocks, typically found under /etc/nginx/conf. d/ on RHEL or /etc/nginx/sites-available/ with symlinks to sites-enabled on Debian. Key directives you will use repeatedly include listen to bind IPs and ports, server_name to match incoming Host headers, root to set the document root for static files, index to list default files, and location blocks to control request handling. For example, a server block listening on port 80 with a root and a try_files pattern is a common way to serve static sites. A common error is confusing root inside nested location blocks; root is inherited but path resolution can differ if alias is used instead. Validate syntax with sudo nginx -t before reloading, since a syntax error can prevent Nginx from starting. As you edit server blocks, think about how specificity in server_name and location affects routing and which block becomes the default for unmatched requests. Nginx Configuration Files and Main Directives means use nginx.conf for globals and server blocks for domain-specific settings; key directives control binding, document roots, and request handling.. In practical terms, understanding nginx.conf, server blocks, and directive roles. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Config structure
keyIdea.text: Use nginx.conf for globals and server blocks for domain-specific settings; key directives control binding, document roots, and request handling.

content.html:
Definition

Files and directives

nginx.conf holds global settings; server blocks define domains and behavior for each site.

listen
Bind address and port, e.g., listen 80; or listen [::]:80; for IPv6.
server_name
Domain names the block responds to; specificity avoids accidental matches.
root & index
Document root and default files like index.html. Use correct paths to avoid 404s.
Example server block
server {
    listen 80;
    listen [::]:80;
    server_name static.example.com www.static.example.com;
    root /var/www/static.example.com/html;
    index index.html index.htm;

    location / {
        try_files $uri $uri/ =404;
    }

    error_log /var/log/nginx/static.example.com_error.log;
    access_log /var/log/nginx/static.example.com_access.log;
}
Misconfiguration pitfall

Using incorrect root paths or misplacing files is the most common cause of site 404s; verify filesystem paths and permissions.

Key Takeaway

Understand directive roles and always test with nginx -t before reloading to avoid service interruption.

screens.title: Server Block for Static Content
screens.subtitle: A working example and why try_files matters

narration.text: A server block for static content is a common Nginx use case. The block defines where Nginx listens, the domain names it responds to, the document root, and default index files. The location / block often uses try_files to attempt serving the exact URI, then the URI as a directory, and finally return a 404 if nothing matches. This prevents arbitrary directory listings and gives predictable behavior. Consider the example server block for static. example. com that sets root to /var/www/static. example. com/html and uses try_files $uri $uri/ =404. A practical example: place an index. html in that document root and request the domain in a browser or via curl to confirm it returns the file. A typical misconception is believing try_files will automatically fall back to a backend; it does not unless you explicitly proxy to a backend in another location. Always set error_log and access_log paths so you can troubleshoot 404s and permission errors. Test the syntax with nginx -t and reload the daemon so your changes take effect without dropping existing connections. Server Block for Static Content means try_files checks file, then directory, then returns a 404; it prevents unintended directory listings and clarifies fallback behavior.. In practical terms, a working example and why try_files matters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: try_files pattern
keyIdea.text: try_files checks file, then directory, then returns a 404; it prevents unintended directory listings and clarifies fallback behavior.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough

Static server block

server {
    listen 80;
    listen [::]:80;
    server_name static.example.com www.static.example.com;
    root /var/www/static.example.com/html;
    index index.html index.htm;

    location / {
        try_files $uri $uri/ =404;
    }

    error_log /var/log/nginx/static.example.com_error.log;
    access_log /var/log/nginx/static.example.com_access.log;
}
Practical steps
  • Create the document root and add an index.html file.
  • Run sudo nginx -t then sudo systemctl reload nginx.
  • Use curl or a browser to confirm the index page loads.
Example scenario
You have many static assets to serve for a marketing site. Point static.example.com at your server, place files under the configured root, and let Nginx efficiently serve them to many users.
Misconception
try_files does not proxy to a backend automatically; you must configure a separate location with proxy_pass if you want fallback to an app server.
Key Takeaway

Use try_files for predictable static file resolution and always validate config syntax before reloading.

screens.title: Nginx as a Reverse Proxy
screens.subtitle: Forward requests to backend applications and preserve client info

narration.text: Using Nginx as a reverse proxy means it accepts client requests and forwards them to backend application servers, then returns responses to the client. The core directive is proxy_pass, which points to the backend address and port. Equally important are proxy_set_header directives that pass original request details to the backend, such as Host, X-Real-IP, X-Forwarded-For, and X-Forwarded-Proto. A concrete configuration for app. example. com forwards to localhost:8080 and sets these headers so the backend can log the original client IP and host. A common operational mistake is omitting proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr; without it, backend logs show the proxy server IP instead of the real client address. Always test with nginx -t and use curl with -I or verbose headers to confirm that requests are forwarded and that the backend receives the expected headers. Consider security and trust boundaries: only forward trusted headers to backends you control, and be mindful of header spoofing when exposing proxies publicly. Nginx as a Reverse Proxy means proxy_pass forwards requests; proxy_set_header preserves original host and client ip so backends receive accurate context.. In practical terms, forward requests to backend applications and preserve client info. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Proxy essentials
keyIdea.text: proxy_pass forwards requests; proxy_set_header preserves original host and client IP so backends receive accurate context.

content.html:
Process Flow

Reverse proxy example

server {
    listen 80;
    server_name app.example.com;

    location / {
        proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:5000;
        proxy_set_header Host $host;
        proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;
    }

    error_log /var/log/nginx/app.example.com_error.log;
    access_log /var/log/nginx/app.example.com_access.log;
}
Verification
  • Use curl to request app.example.com and inspect headers.
  • On the backend, check logs for X-Real-IP and Host values.
Example: Flask backend
from flask import Flask, request

app = Flask(__name__)

@app.route('/')
def hello():
    return f"Hello from Flask! Host: {request.headers.get('Host')}, IP: {request.headers.get('X-Real-IP')}
"

if __name__ == '__main__':
    app.run(host='127.0.0.1', port=5000)
Operational note
Always include proxy_set_header directives when backends rely on Host and client IP for logging, security, or routing.
Key Takeaway

Missing proxy_set_header entries commonly cause backends to see only the proxy's IP and lose original request context.

screens.title: Validate and Reload — nginx -t and graceful reload
screens.subtitle: Safe configuration changes and runtime validation

narration.text: Small syntax errors can take Nginx offline if you attempt to restart without validation. The recommended practice is to test the configuration with sudo nginx -t after editing files. This checks syntax and file references and reports any errors or warnings. If the test is successful, apply changes with sudo systemctl reload nginx which performs a graceful reload: worker processes finish current requests and then new workers load the updated configuration without dropping active connections. A concrete troubleshooting example: if a new server block contains a duplicate listen directive or an invalid root path, nginx -t will report the line number and error so you can fix it before reloading. A common misconception is that systemctl restart is always safe; restart terminates and starts workers and may briefly drop connections. Prefer reload for live updates, and restart only when necessary. Also consider logging levels and test with curl or in a browser after a successful reload to confirm behavior. Validate and Reload — nginx -t and graceful reload means always run nginx -t to check syntax, then use systemctl reload for a graceful, zero-downtime configuration update when possible.. In practical terms, safe configuration changes and runtime validation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Safe deploy
keyIdea.text: Always run nginx -t to check syntax, then use systemctl reload for a graceful, zero-downtime configuration update when possible.

content.html:
Definition

Test then reload

Validate with nginx -t, then reload to apply changes without dropping active connections.

Commands
sudo nginx -t
sudo systemctl reload nginx
# Or to restart fully
sudo systemctl restart nginx
Troubleshooting example
If nginx -t reports a duplicate listen or invalid path, fix the indicated file and line before reloading. Review error_log for context if failures persist.
Misconception
Restarting is not always harmless; reload is safer for live workloads because it preserves existing connections.
Key Takeaway

Use nginx -t as a gatekeeper before reloading to avoid configuration-induced downtime.

narration.text: Nginx can perform basic load balancing by defining an upstream block that lists backend servers and then proxying requests to that upstream from a server block. The default method is round-robin, distributing requests evenly across the pool. For example, define upstream app_pool { server 10.0.0.11:5000; server 10.0.0.12:5000; } and then use proxy_pass http://app_pool; in the location block. This pattern is useful when you have multiple app instances on different hosts or ports. Remember to include proxy_set_header directives so each backend knows the original Host and client IP. A common misconception is that Nginx will perform sophisticated health checks by default; basic Nginx requires additional modules or configuration for active health checks. For simple setups, ensure backends return health-friendly responses and monitor logs. Test distribution by sending repeated requests and observing backend logs or responses. Load balancing through Nginx centralizes edge responsibilities like SSL termination and can simplify backend deployment. Basic Load Balancing with upstream means use upstream blocks to group backends and proxy_pass to the pool for simple round-robin load distribution; add health checks if needed.. In practical terms, distribute requests across backend servers. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Upstream pool
keyIdea.text: Use upstream blocks to group backends and proxy_pass to the pool for simple round-robin load distribution; add health checks if needed.

content.html:
Architecture

Upstream example

upstream app_pool {
    server 10.0.0.11:5000;
    server 10.0.0.12:5000;
}

server {
    listen 80;
    server_name app.example.com;

    location / {
        proxy_pass http://app_pool;
        proxy_set_header Host $host;
        proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
    }
}
Verification
  • Send repeated requests and check which backend logged each request.
  • Consider sticky sessions only when backend state requires it.
Operational note
Nginx provides basic load balancing out of the box. For active health checks or advanced algorithms, add the proper modules or use a dedicated balancer.
Misconception
Default Nginx does not perform active health checks of backends without additional configuration or modules.
Key Takeaway

Upstream blocks enable simple round-robin balancing; plan monitoring or health checks depending on production needs.

screens.title: Apache vs Nginx — Use Cases and Differences
screens.subtitle: Choosing the right tool for static, dynamic, and hybrid deployments

narration.text: Comparing Apache and Nginx helps you choose the right tool for each job. Apache historically uses process-per-connection or threaded models controlled by MPMs, and it supports per-directory configuration with. htaccess. This makes Apache flexible for shared hosting and situations where administrators require directory-level overrides. Nginx, by contrast, uses an event-driven, asynchronous model and centralizes configuration, which improves performance for static content and high concurrency. A practical hybrid approach is to put Nginx at the edge to serve static assets and terminate SSL, then proxy dynamic requests to Apache running PHP or other dynamic modules. A misconception to avoid is thinking one server always rules: instead, design a stack that leverages strengths — Nginx for statics and proxying, Apache for legacy modules and certain dynamic workflows. As an LFCE, you will often encounter architectures using both together; your role is to configure routing, headers, and security so both servers work as a unified service. Apache vs Nginx — Use Cases and Differences means use nginx for high-concurrency static serving and proxying; use apache when per-directory overrides or certain modules are required, or combine both as needed.. In practical terms, choosing the right tool for static, dynamic, and hybrid deployments. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Best of both
keyIdea.text: Use Nginx for high-concurrency static serving and proxying; use Apache when per-directory overrides or certain modules are required, or combine both as needed.

content.html:
Comparison

Apache vs Nginx

Apache
Process/thread-based models, supports .htaccess, and is often used for dynamic modules like mod_php. Good for shared-host and legacy applications requiring per-directory overrides.
When to use
  • Applications relying on Apache modules
  • Environments needing directory-level overrides
Nginx
Event-driven, non-blocking, and efficient for static files, concurrency, reverse proxying, and load balancing. Centralized configuration improves performance but requires sudo to edit.
When to use
  • Static asset delivery at scale
  • Edge reverse proxy and SSL termination
Key Takeaway

Combine servers when appropriate: Nginx excels at fronting traffic and serving static assets while Apache can handle legacy dynamic workloads.

screens.title: Common Mistakes, Firewall, and SELinux Considerations
screens.subtitle: Troubleshooting the usual operational pitfalls

narration.text: Operationally, several mistakes recur when configuring Nginx. First, forgetting to run nginx -t before reloading can bring down service due to syntax errors. Second, incorrect root or proxy_pass paths cause 404s or failed backend connections; verify filesystem paths and backend reachability. Third, firewall rules may block ports 80 and 443 even if Nginx is running; ensure firewall-cmd or UFW rules allow HTTP and HTTPS. On RHEL systems, SELinux contexts are another common source of failures: custom document roots or log directories may require proper file contexts such as httpd_sys_content_t for web files and httpd_log_t for logs; reverse proxying to network services may require enabling the httpd_can_network_connect boolean. A frequent misconception is assuming SELinux is irrelevant; instead, misconfigured contexts often silently block access. When troubleshooting, check nginx error logs, systemctl status, firewall rules, and SELinux messages. The final step is verifying headers from the backend to ensure proxy_set_header directives are present when required. Common Mistakes, Firewall, and SELinux Considerations means always run nginx -t, verify firewall rules, check selinux contexts on rhel, and confirm proxy headers are present when needed by backends.. In practical terms, troubleshooting the usual operational pitfalls. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Operational checklist
keyIdea.text: Always run nginx -t, verify firewall rules, check SELinux contexts on RHEL, and confirm proxy headers are present when needed by backends.

content.html:
Core Concept

Common mistakes and safety notes

Missing nginx -t
Validate configuration before reloading to avoid service outage due to a syntax error.
Firewall blocking ports
Confirm firewall-cmd or UFW allows HTTP/HTTPS even if the service is active.
SELinux contexts (RHEL)
Adjust contexts for custom roots and enable httpd_can_network_connect for reverse proxying when required.
Incorrect root or proxy_pass
Double-check path correctness and backend addresses to avoid 404s and connection failures.
Missing proxy_set_header
Backends will see the proxy IP unless headers like X-Real-IP and X-Forwarded-For are forwarded.
server_name conflicts
Be explicit with server_name to prevent unintended routing to the default server block.
Key Takeaway

Follow a checklist: syntax test, firewall, SELinux context, correct paths, and proxy headers to avoid common failures.

screens.title: Lab Walkthrough: Static Site and Flask Reverse Proxy
screens.subtitle: Step-by-step terminal tasks to complete the hands-on activity

narration.text: This walkthrough guides the lab in a terminal-first fashion. Step one: install Nginx on your distro, ensuring EPEL is enabled for RHEL if needed. Step two: create /var/www/static. example. com/html, place an index. html file, and create a server block using the static example. Test with nginx -t and reload, then curl the domain after mapping it in /etc/hosts to your server IP. Step three: install Python and Flask, create the provided app dot P Y file that returns the Host and X-Real-IP headers, and run it on 127.0.0.1:5000. Step four: create a second server block for app. example. com that proxy_passes to 127.0.0.1:5000 and includes proxy_set_header Host $host and X-Real-IP $remote_addr. After nginx -t and reload, access app. example. com and confirm the Flask response shows the original Host and IP. screens.title: Assessment: Diagnose Missing Client IP in Backend Logs
screens.subtitle: Identify the directive that passes client IP through a proxy

narration.text: A common assessment scenario is diagnosing why a backend application logs the proxy server's IP instead of the original client's IP. The core cause is usually missing or incorrect proxy_set_header directives. To diagnose, check the Nginx location block that proxies to the backend and look for proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr and proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for. If these are absent, the backend will only see the proxy IP. A practical troubleshooting approach: curl the proxy and then inspect backend logs; if the IP is the proxy, add the header directives and reload Nginx after running nginx -t. Also ensure that intermediary load balancers or CDNs are not overwriting headers, and that backends read X-Real-IP or X-Forwarded-For depending on your app. The assessment checks your ability to read configuration, recognize the missing header pattern, and apply the correct fix while verifying results with a test request. content.html:
Assessment Idea

Diagnose missing client IP

Symptoms
Backend logs show requests coming from the proxy server IP rather than the original client addresses.
Root cause
proxy_set_header directives are missing or misconfigured in the Nginx location block that forwards requests.
Fix
proxy_set_header Host $host;
proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;
Verification
After adding headers, run nginx -t, reload, then curl and check backend logs for the original client IP entries.
Key Takeaway

Passing client headers to backends is essential for correct logging and security-related logic; proxy_set_header is the directive to check.

narration.text: Here are the essential concepts to keep in mind. First, Nginx is an event-driven web server and proxy that excels at serving static content and handling high concurrency. Second, server blocks are Nginx's per-site configuration units; they define listen, server_name, root, index, and location behavior. Third, when acting as a reverse proxy, proxy_pass forwards requests to backends and proxy_set_header ensures backends receive original host and client IP data. Remember to validate configurations with nginx -t and prefer graceful reloads to avoid dropped connections. Finally, basic load balancing is done with upstream blocks and proxy_pass to the pool; consider health checks and monitoring for production. Keep these concepts focused when you configure Nginx: architecture, server blocks, proxy headers, validation, and upstream balancing.
